newsitem.title: USA: Princess Di invades White House.
newsitem.headline: Princess Di invades White House.

text.p: She only smiled and didn't speak, but Princess Diana on Tuesday led what first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton called "one of the nicest British invasions" of the White House.

Mrs. Clinton, drawing attention to efforts in the fight against breast cancer, hosted an elegant East Room breakfast featuring Napoleon of herbed eggs and roasted tomatoes for a select guest list that ranged from fashion designers to media moguls.

Officially, the princess was only the honorary chairwoman of a fundraising effort to support cancer research. In reality, most of the 122 people sitting under the ornate crystal chandeliers gave royal treatment to the woman who is no longer formally part of British royalty.

"I was thinking as I met her in the Blue Room that this is one of the nicest British invasions that the White House has ever had," Mrs. Clinton said. "The other one, some of you may remember from history, burned the place down."
"But now we have the metaphorical equivalent of that excitement here in the White House," she said.

Mrs. Clinton made her remarks standing before a famous Gilbert Stuart oil painting of the nation's first president, George Washington, which was rescued by then-first lady Dolley Madison when British forces burned the White House during the War of 1812.
The current first lady, who like her honoured guest has come under the unflattering glare of media scrutiny, offered praise for the former spouse of Prince Charles, heir to the British throne.

"She is a woman who has had a tireless committment to the homeless, AIDS, cancer, leprosy and other health issues and we are so pleased that she is lending her support to this continuing fight against breast cancer," Mrs. Clinton said.
Diana, wearing a dark chocolate, double-breasted, pin striped coat dress and a necklace of large pearls, smiled and nodded but never spoke. She didn't have to.
Like a maestro leading an attentive orchestra, every time she tilted her head or changed her expression, a band of photographers filled the room with a chorus of shutter clicks.
Most of the fashionably dressed breakfast participants, who included designers Oscar de la Renta and Ralph Lauren, sat up straight in their chairs to catch a better look.
Mrs. Clinton wore a sea blue business suit by de la Renta, even though Lauren is a co-chairman of the fundraiser that brought Diana to Washington.

She is serving as the honorary chairwoman of a $500-a-person evening gala to raise funds for the Nina Hyde Breast Cancer Centre, named after a fashion editor at the Washington Post who died of breast cancer in 1990.
Katharine Graham, who chairs the board of The Washington Post Company, and Lauren were co-chairs of the fundraising dinner.
